compression.title: Canaries Dashboard (Canaries in the Coal Mine?)
compression.lede: is the Stanford Digital Economy Lab's monthly dashboard with ADP Research, and the working paper it extends (Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen): employment by age and AI exposure in ADP payroll records, an observed outcome on the distribution of gains and losses (census record); early, descriptive indicators, not causal estimates (the paper).

sentences.text: The Canaries Dashboard is an observed-employment-outcome resource on the distribution of gains and losses, a working paper and monthly-updated dashboard among the Stanford Digital Economy Lab's AI Economic Indicators (Labor Vector census record), which in its own words summarizes, in collaboration with ADP Research, "live labor market trends for a sample workers in firms using ADP payroll services" (the dashboard).

The dashboard updates and extends the working paper "Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence" by Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen (the dashboard; the paper's page), first released in August 2025 and revised on 12 August 2026 (the paper; census record), and the census lists the paper's title and the bare phrase among the entity's names (census record).

The name is the idiom put to work: the authors write that generative AI's "proficiency with codified knowledge work" suggests "there may be “canaries in the coal mine” which will be affected first" (the paper), and the dashboard calls its granular, timely results "an early signal of changes to the labor market, a canary in the coal mine", complementing rather than substituting for analyses of nationally representative data (the dashboard).

On the dashboard's premise, "specific segments of the labor market can provide a leading indicator of employment trends for the broader economy" (the dashboard), and Bharat Chandar's page describes the work as "tracking “canaries in the coal mine” for entry-level employment changes in jobs exposed to AI" (the paper's page).

The bare phrase is therefore a homonym of the study by construction, the paper's question mark marking its title as a use of the idiom, and the phrase is an idiom before it is a title (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the name is also the idiom's (Capture Registry), and Wikipedia resolves the idiom to its article "Sentinel species", section "Canaries", not to the study (Wikipedia).

Its operator is the Stanford Digital Economy Lab with ADP Research, the paper by Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (census record), and the dashboard asks to be cited as the Stanford Digital Economy Lab and ADP Research's "AI Economic Indicators: Canaries Dashboard" (the dashboard).

The paper uses "high-frequency administrative payroll data from ADP covering millions of U.S. workers through June 2026" to document six facts about the labor market after the adoption of generative AI, and balances "timeliness, worker granularity, and administrative verifiability"; ADP serves firms employing over 26 million U.S. workers, and the analysis panel holds between 3.5 and 5 million employees a month (the paper).

The dashboard adopts the paper's balanced sample, firms with five years of employment history in ADP, rolled forward monthly and limited to workers matched to an occupation code: at launch 25,000 firms, 4.6 million matched workers in November 2022 and over 730 occupations (the dashboard; census record), employment indexed from November 2022 and descriptive indices beside event-study regressions (census record).

Whose labor it observes the census gives as the employment of these workers grouped by age and by their occupation's AI exposure, the labor supplied by "workers in firms using ADP payroll services (the payroll records)" (census record).

Exposure is matched from "Eloundou et al. (2024) and the Anthropic Economic Index" (the dashboard), so the dashboard is not itself a usage measure (census record) and takes from the index its augmentation and automation ratios by occupation (census record); in the index's terms as the dashboard gives them, "users fully delegate tasks" under automation, while augmentation "features collaboration between humans and an AI system" (the dashboard).
The paper finds "no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement" (the paper; census record).

Its headline is that employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations "now stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with that of their less-exposed peers", experienced workers showing "no comparable gap" (the paper; census record); in levels, that age group fell about 11% in the two most exposed quintiles from November 2022 to June 2026 and grew about 10% in the three least exposed (the paper).

The divergence "has widened steadily since we first documented it in August 2025", operates "primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations", and adjusts "through employment rather than base compensation" (the paper).

The census reads this as a record of costs, the shortfall of young workers' employment in exposed occupations with adjustment through employment, and records who directs the hiring as not recorded and who receives the gains as not recorded, which the evidence cannot settle (census record).

Declines concentrate "in occupations where AI usage primarily substitutes for human tasks", while where usage complements workers employment is "flat or rising, especially for experienced workers" (the paper; census record); on the dashboard the complementarity share shows no clear monotonic relationship with employment trends, while the automation ratio "shows a clear correlation with employment trends" (the dashboard; census record).

The dashboard draws from this that "the character of AI usage could shape the labor market effects of AI" (the dashboard), and the census reads the same grouping, borrowed from the Anthropic Economic Index, as "where a usage measure of who directs the task meets an observed employment outcome", which the resource itself reads as correlation (census record).

The archive's Provenance Erasure Rate paper names the channels AI-economics research measures, labor displacement among them, as frameworks that "measure which jobs AI eliminates, what tasks it can perform, and what consumer surplus it generates", and sets beside them a channel where human labor remains and the value tied to provenance is extracted: "This is not displacement; it is extraction without attribution" (#716).

It names that fourth channel compositional authority transfer, "the rate at which AI synthesis captures value from human authors by stripping the attribution that would otherwise carry economic weight" (#716).

The paper offers "suggestive evidence about mechanisms", declines for young workers in occupations that involve codified knowledge, and as "One possibility" that AI substitutes for codified knowledge while complementing the tacit knowledge of senior employees; the entry-level hiring slowdown "provides early suggestions that generative AI may be affecting the career ladder" (the paper).

Women face greater AI exposure on average (the paper); early-career women in the most-exposed quintile have seen employment contract 4.5% a year since November 2022 against 2.5% for men, a difference the dashboard finds "driven primarily by occupational composition" (the dashboard, updated 22 July 2026; census record), and early-career software developers and customer service workers show substantial declines while home health aides grow for the youngest (the dashboard).

The divergence persists when excluding technology firms and computer occupations, when controlling for interest-rate exposure and remote work, and across alternative exposure measures, and is robust to allowing firm entry and exit (the paper); with the broadest set of controls, declines in exposed occupations become statistically significant in 2024, the earlier declines "likely driven by non-AI factors" (the dashboard, from the February 2026 update).

The authors interpret the facts "as early, descriptive indicators—canaries in the coal mine—rather than causal estimates" and caution that the work "does not estimate a causal impact of AI"; the patterns attenuate with education controls, show some divergence predating generative AI and are more pronounced in the ADP sample than in national survey benchmarks, and the authors make no predictions (the paper).

The dashboard "measures the correlation between occupational exposure measures and employment trends in our sample, rather than a causal link between the two" (the dashboard), and the census carries the limit with what the evidence cannot settle: "whether AI exposure causes the employment change" (census record).

Its sample is "large, but not necessarily representative" and "represents neither the entire U.S. labor market nor the universe of firms using ADP payroll services", the balanced sample "shuts down the margins of firm entry and exit" (the dashboard; census record), and there may be selection in which firms use ADP (the paper).

Earlier versions headlined regression estimates, a 13% relative decline at July 2025 data and 16% at September 2025 data, and the August 2026 revision emphasizes the descriptive divergence, 15% at the July 2025 vintage and 19% as of June 2026 (the paper), after a February 2026 update addressing the response to the paper and on a larger set of data (the paper's page).

The dashboard was "Last updated October 21, 2026" and is updated monthly, with "an expanded and reweighted sample" announced (the dashboard; census record); earlier versions of the paper are available by email (the paper's page; census record), its license is not stated in the saved text, and the census left the PDF, the chart data, the authors' notes and the license unchecked (census record).

The census asks of it its organizing question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?", and places it in two worked questions, as observed employment change set against exposure estimates and as costs observed where no record measures the distribution of productivity gains (census record).

At the bare name on 29 October 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the idiom and carried the study, the Lab's Canaries Dashboard with ADP Research, in one bullet, "at the grain of its subject (young workers' employment as an early indicator)": the Lab named, no author, no identifier, the paper's page cited as card 1, with "early indicators" the record's own frame and no causal or displacement claim made (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The finding, the dashboard and its limits are absent; "An idiom outranks the study named after it, which survives as an example of the idiom's use"; the generic sense is the target's own frame turned outward and is not carried to devalue the study; the registry reads that the record would be reached at its title with its question mark or at the Lab's name; and no card cites the census record (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Wikipedia has no article on the paper, the dashboard or the Lab; three articles cite the paper, "AI takeover" with the August 2025 version's 13% relative decline, "Artificial intelligence" with decreasing employment rates for early-career workers, and "Silicon Valley" with the 19% gap, which it sets against "older, less exposed workers" where the paper compares less-exposed peers (Wikipedia; the paper).

O716-01.quote: AI economics research focuses primarily on labor displacement (Acemoglu and Restrepo 2019), capability projection (Eloundou et al. 2023), and welfare estimation (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond 2023). These frameworks measure which jobs AI eliminates, what tasks it can perform, and what consumer surplus it generates. PER identifies a distinct channel: even when human labor *remains* (the author's work is used), the economic value tied to provenance — reputation, traffic, citation credit, contractual rights — is extracted by the system. This is not displacement; it is extraction without attribution.
O716-01.source_label: #716 Provenance Erasure Rate A Compression-Survival Metric for Attribution Loss in AI-Composed Search Outputs
O716-01.locus: §2.2 ¶ 'AI economics research focuses primarily on labor displacement'

O716-02.quote: Existing AI-economics research addresses three channels: labor displacement, capability projection, and welfare estimation. PER addresses a fourth: **compositional authority transfer** — the rate at which AI synthesis captures value from human authors by stripping the attribution that would otherwise carry economic weight.

CAP-1-01.quote: The record's entity is the Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries Dashboard with ADP Research, from the paper 'Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence'.

CAP-1-02.quote: The composition carries the study in one bullet, at the grain of its subject (young workers' employment as an early indicator).

CAP-1-11.quote: The Stanford Digital Economy Lab named; no author; no identifier; the paper's page cited (card 1).

CAP-1-12.quote: Claim boundary present beneath the gate: 'early indicators' is the record's own frame ('early, descriptive indicators—canaries in the coal mine—rather than causal estimates') and the bullet makes no causal or displacement claim; the findings (no economy-wide displacement; workers 22-25 in exposed occupations 19% below trend; through hiring) and the sample limits are not carried.

CAP-1-03.quote: THE FINDING ABSENT. The record's headline: employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, through reduced hiring, with no comparable gap for experienced workers and no evidence of economy-wide displacement.

CAP-1-04.quote: THE DASHBOARD AND ITS LIMITS ABSENT. The monthly dashboard (last updated 21 October 2026), its ADP sample and its own statement that the indicators are early, descriptive and not causal are not composed.

CAP-1-07.quote: An idiom outranks the study named after it, which survives as an example of the idiom's use.

CAP-1-13.quote: The record's own title borrows the idiom, so the generic sense is the target's own frame turned outward; this is recorded here, and not as an inversion, since the idiom is not carried to devalue the study.

CAP-1-08.quote: The record would be reached at its title with its question mark or with the lab's name; the bare phrase gives the composition layer's account of the study as a figure of speech.

CAP-1-09.quote: A baseline: the record landed on laborvector.org the same day (commit bf90841) and no card cites it.
